content: When the LORD invited Solomon to ask anything, what did he ask for?
explanation: 1 Kings 3:9 records Solomon's request: 'Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?' Therefore, the correct answer is to ask for wisdom (an understanding heart) to judge the people. Distractor 1 (Wealth) is incorrect because Solomon was granted wealth afterward (1 Kings 3:11-13), not what he directly asked for. Distractor 2 (Wisdom to build a temple) is 'close' but incorrect in a key detail: the purpose for which he asked for wisdom is clearly for 'judging the people,' not for building (the temple construction is mentioned in later passages). Distractor 3 (Long life) is a common misunderstanding (often a general human desire), but it was not what Solomon requested in this situation.
options: Wisdom to govern the people
Wealth to bestow upon the people
Wisdom to build a temple for God
Long life for himself

content: On Mount Carmel, when Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal, what happened?
explanation:
Correct answer: 1 Kings 18:38 records: 'Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.' Verse 39 shows the result: 'And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, "The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God."'

Analysis of incorrect answers:
1. 'Fire from the altar flared up and consumed the sacrifice' (Incorrect detail): The fire came from heaven, not from the altar Elijah had built (v.38).
2. 'An earthquake shook the mountain' (Incorrect scope): The earthquake appears in Elijah's vision in 1 Kings 19:11-12, not in this event.
3. 'The prophets of Baal acknowledged Elijah as the true prophet' (Wrong nearby passage): The people acknowledged the LORD (v.39), while the prophets of Baal were seized and killed (v.40), not acknowledging Elijah.
options: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering
Fire from the altar flared up and consumed the sacrifice
An earthquake shook the mountain
The prophets of Baal acknowledged Elijah as the true prophet

content: How long did it take Solomon to build the temple?
explanation: 1 Kings 6:38 — The temple was built in seven years. A magnificent work.
options: 40 years
3 years
7 years
12 years

content: At the dedication of the temple, what did Solomon declare about God?
explanation:
1 Kings 8:27 records Solomon's prayer: 'But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!' This verse emphasizes the immeasurable greatness of God, far surpassing any physical temple. The correct answer faithfully quotes this idea.

The incorrect answers: (1) '...much less Jerusalem' is close but misstates a key detail (replacing 'this house' with 'Jerusalem'), losing the direct contrast with the temple just built. (2) 'The LORD will dwell in this temple forever' is incorrect in scope — Solomon prays for God to hear from the temple (v.29), but does not declare He will dwell there forever; on the contrary, v.27 emphasizes God is not limited to it. (3) 'This is the place God chose for the Israelites to worship Him,' while true to the general context (God chose Jerusalem), misses the point of the question — the question asks about Solomon's statement *concerning God's nature* in v.27, not about the temple's purpose.
options: Even the highest heavens cannot contain you, much less Jerusalem
The LORD will dwell in this temple forever
Heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain You — much less this house
This is the place God chose for the Israelites to worship Him

content: From which land did the queen come to test Solomon's wisdom?
explanation: The Scripture passage 1 Kings 10:1-9 clearly states: 'Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon... she came to Jerusalem' (verse 1). Therefore, the correct answer is 'Queen of Sheba'. Distractor 1 (Assyria) is incorrect because Assyria is a neighboring empire often mentioned in the books of the Prophets and Kings, but it is not the queen in this passage. Distractor 2 (Pharaoh) is incorrect because this is a common misunderstanding—Pharaoh is the title of the king of Egypt, not a queen, and 1 Kings 3:1 mentions Pharaoh's daughter who married Solomon, but she is not the one who came to test his wisdom. Distractor 3 (Judah) is incorrect because Judah was Solomon's own kingdom, not a foreign kingdom with a queen who visited.
options: Queen of Sheba
Queen of Assyria
Queen of Pharaoh
Queen of Judah

content: Why did Solomon fall in his later years?
explanation: 1 Kings 11:4 records: 'For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.' Therefore, the correct answer is due to the influence of his foreign wives. Distractor 1 ('His court officials') is close but incorrect in the specific subject (it is close to descriptions of the court but not the cause in this verse). Distractor 2 is incorrect in scope because the hoarding of gold and silver (1 Kings 10:14-27), though an ostentation, was not the direct cause leading to his idolatrous downfall. Distractor 3 is a common misunderstanding because there is no specific record of a prophecy directly warning Solomon before this event; God's warning is recorded afterward (1 Kings 11:9-13).
options: His foreign wives turned his heart away to other gods
His court officials urged him to worship idols
He fell because he wanted to hoard much gold and silver
He ignored a prior prophetic warning from God

content: Whose fault was it that the kingdom split?
explanation:
1 Kings 12:16-19 records the event: when all Israel saw that King Rehoboam would not listen to them, they answered, 'What share do we have in David? ... To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!' So Israel rebelled, and only Judah remained loyal. The correct answer is Rehoboam, because his refusal to lighten the people's burden (verses 13-14) directly caused the kingdom to split.

Incorrect answers: 1) Jeroboam, though later made king by the people, was not the direct cause of the split; the split occurred due to the people's reaction to Rehoboam's decision. 2) The elders gave correct advice (verses 6-7), but Rehoboam did not listen; they are not at fault. 3) David is mentioned in the people's response, but this split was a direct consequence of Rehoboam's contemporary actions, not due to David's past sins.
options: Rehoboam, for refusing to lighten the people's burden
Jeroboam, because he initiated the opposition to Rehoboam
The elders, because they advised Rehoboam to speak kindly to the people
David, because of his past sins

content: What did the LORD use to feed Elijah by the brook Cherith?
explanation:
Correct answer: 'Ravens brought bread and meat to him' (1 Kings 17:4-6). The LORD said He had commanded the ravens to feed Elijah there, and they brought him bread and meat every morning and evening.

Explanation of incorrect answers:
- 'Angels brought bread and meat to him': Incorrect detail. This Scripture passage only mentions ravens, not angels. This is a 'close but wrong' distractor because angels are often present in other miracles, but not in this specific context.
- 'Nearby villagers brought food to him': Incorrect scope/circumstance. The LORD commanded Elijah to hide by the Brook Cherith, isolated from people, to be supernaturally fed by ravens.
- 'Elijah found bread and meat by the brook himself': Misses the point. The question asks 'What did God use to feed Elijah?', focusing on the means God employed. This option describes the food source passively, not the agent God used to provide it.
options: Angels brought bread and meat to him
Nearby villagers brought food to him
Ravens bringing bread and meat
Elijah found bread and meat by the brook himself

content: What miracle happened to the widow of Zarephath?
explanation:
The question directly asks about the miracle that happened to the widow of Zarephath in 1 Kings 17:14-16. The Scripture clearly states: 'The jar of flour will not be used up and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain on the land.' (verse 14), and it happened exactly as promised (verse 16). This was a continuous miracle throughout the famine.

Distractor 1 (close but incorrect, error type 'wrong_detail') is wrong because the miracle was a continuous supernatural provision, not just a one-time filling. Distractor 2 (error type 'wrong_scope') is wrong because it relates to a different type of miracle (field provision) not mentioned in this passage. Distractor 3 (error type 'common_misconception') is wrong because the healing miracle for her son (resurrection) occurs in the later passage (1 Kings 17:17-24), not in the content of this question (17:14-16).
options: The jar of flour and the jug of oil became full only once
Jar of flour and jug of oil did not run out throughout the famine
The woman and her son ate continuously from their own field
Her son was healed from a serious illness

content: After his victory on Mount Carmel, how did Elijah react when Jezebel threatened him?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER: 'Was afraid and fled into the wilderness, wishing to die' (1 Kings 19:3-4). After receiving the news, Elijah 'was afraid and arose and ran for his life' (verse 3), went into the wilderness, sat under a broom tree, and prayed that he might die (verse 4).

EXPLANATION OF INCORRECT ANSWERS:
1. 'Prayed for God to send fire to destroy Jezebel': Close but incorrect in a key detail. This was Elijah's action against the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:36-40), not his reaction upon hearing Jezebel's threat.
2. 'Joyfully built an altar to worship the LORD': Incorrect scope. This action belongs to the earlier event on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:30-32), and his state of mind then was one of determination, not his reaction after the threat.
3. 'Stayed and challenged Jezebel to a confrontation': A common misconception based on Elijah's previous strong image. In reality, Scripture clearly states he was afraid and fled immediately, with no challenging action following the threat.
options: Fled in fear into the wilderness, asking to die
Prayed for God to send fire to destroy Jezebel
Joyfully built an altar to worship the LORD
Stayed and challenged Jezebel to a confrontation

content: How did the LORD appear to Elijah at Mount Horeb?
explanation:
The question asks about the means through which the LORD spoke to Elijah AFTER the phenomena of the great wind, earthquake, and fire (1 Kings 19:11-12). The correct answer is 'A still small voice (a gentle whisper)' (verse 12).

- Distractor 'The sound of a great wind striking the mountain' (close but incorrect): Wrong because this is the first phenomenon that occurred BEFORE the LORD spoke, described in verse 11. It is part of the sequence of events, but it is not the means the LORD used to speak finally.
- Distractor 'The sound of a roaring earthquake': Wrong because this is the second phenomenon that occurred BEFORE, described in verse 11. The LORD was not in the earthquake.
- Distractor 'The sound of a raging fire': Wrong because this is the third phenomenon that occurred BEFORE, described in verse 12. The LORD was not in the fire either. The question specifically asks about what happened AFTER these three phenomena.
options: The sound of a great wind striking the mountain
A low whisper (still small voice)
The sound of a roaring earthquake
The sound of a raging fire

content: How many had not bowed the knee to Baal, the LORD told Elijah?
explanation:
In 1 Kings 19:18, the LORD said to Elijah: 'Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him.' Therefore, the correct answer is '7,000 people'.
- Distractor '700 people' is close but incorrect in the specific number.
- Distractor '70,000 people' is incorrect in scale, being ten times the right number.
- Distractor 'All Israel never knelt before Baal' is based on a common misunderstanding that the entire nation remained faithful, while the text refers only to a remnant.
options: 700 people
70,000 people
All Israel never knelt before Baal

content: How did Elijah call Elisha to be his disciple?
explanation:
In 1 Kings 19:19-21, Elijah meets Elisha while he is plowing, goes over to him, and throws his cloak on him (verse 19). This is a symbolic act to call him as a disciple. Elisha understands and runs after Elijah. *The correct answer is correct because it accurately describes the key action recorded.*

The incorrect answers:
1. 'Through a prophecy from an angel's mouth': Incorrect because it belongs to a nearby passage. In this specific passage and just before it (verses 5-18), Elijah interacts with an angel and hears God's voice, but the calling of Elisha does not involve any angel.
2. 'Inviting him to a meal at Elisha's house': Incorrect detail. In verse 21, it is Elisha who slaughters the oxen, cooks the meat, feeds the people, and then follows Elijah, not Elijah inviting him to a meal at Elisha's house as a way to call him.
3. 'Laying hands on his head and praying': Incorrect due to a common misconception. The act of laying on hands is often associated with ordination or blessing in Scripture, but in this specific context, the method used is 'throwing the cloak.' This is a 'close but incorrect' distractor because it relates to a familiar calling/transfer ritual, but misses the key detail about the action.
options: Cast his cloak upon Elisha
Through a prophecy from an angel's mouth
Inviting him to a meal at Elisha's house
Laying hands on his head and praying

content: Who anointed Solomon king over Israel?
explanation: In 1 Kings 1:39, Priest Zadok took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon, causing the people to shout, 'Long live King Solomon!'. Option 1 (Abiathar) is incorrect because, although he was also a priest and present in this passage (verses 7, 25), it was Zadok who performed the anointing ceremony. Option 2 (Nathan) is incorrect because he was the prophet who played a key role in informing David and supporting Solomon (verses 11-27, 32-34), but he was not the one who anointed. Option 3 (King David) is incorrect because, although he was the father and the one who appointed Solomon as king (verses 30, 35), he did not directly perform the anointing ceremony; this is a common misunderstanding that the father-king would directly transfer royal authority.
options: Priest Abiathar
Prophet Nathan
King David
Zadok the priest

content: Whose wisdom did 1 Kings 4:29-30 say Solomon's wisdom surpassed?
explanation:
1 Kings 4:30 clearly states: 'Solomon's wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the people of the East, and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt.' Therefore, the correct answer is 'Greater than all the people of the East and Egypt'. 

Distractor 1 is wrong because it replaces 'Egypt' with 'Babylon', a different nation not mentioned in this verse (incorrect detail). 
Distractor 2 is wrong because it unnecessarily broadens the scope ('the neighboring countries') instead of specifying 'Egypt' as the Bible records (incorrect scope). 
Distractor 3 is wrong because although 'the people of Gad' appear in the list of district governors in the preceding verses (1 Kings 4:13-19), they are not related to the comparison of wisdom in verse 30 (correct text but irrelevant to the question).
options: Greater than all the people of the East and Babylon
All people of the east and Egypt
Greater than all the people of the East and the neighboring countries
Greater than all the people of the East and the people of Gad

content: After Solomon finished the temple, what did the LORD promise on condition that he walked with Him?
explanation:
The question asks about the promise the LORD spoke in 1 Kings 9:3-5. The correct answer is 'The royal throne will be established forever' (verse 5).
- Distractor 1 (wrong_scope): 'The house of Israel will be honored among the nations' is a potential blessing but is NOT the specific promise in this passage (3-5); it belongs to the wrong scope (verses 8-9 mention it if they turn away).
- Distractor 2 (common_misconception): 'Trade will flourish everywhere' reflects a common misconception about Solomon's wealth and achievements, but it is NOT part of the specific promise in 1 Kings 9:3-5.
- Distractor 3 (nearby_passage): 'Vows made in the temple will be fulfilled' (verse 3) is textually correct from the earlier part of the passage (specifically verse 3), but it misses the point of the question because the question asks about the promise the LORD MADE to Solomon, whereas this describes the LORD HEARING prayer.
options: The house of Israel will be honored among the nations
Trade will flourish everywhere
An everlasting royal throne
Vows made in the temple will be fulfilled

content: The prophet Ahijah tore his garment into 12 pieces and gave Jeroboam how many?
explanation:
In 1 Kings 11:31, Ahijah said to Jeroboam, 'Take for yourself ten pieces; for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon and give you ten tribes."' The correct answer is ten pieces (10 tribes).

- The distractor 'Eleven pieces (11 tribes)' is incorrect because it deviates by one in the quantity compared to the Bible (10 vs. 11).
- The distractor 'Twelve pieces (2 tribes)' is incorrect due to a misunderstanding of scope: although 12 is the correct total number of pieces, the number of tribes (2) refers to the portion reserved for the house of David, not the quantity given to Jeroboam.
- The distractor 'One piece (all 12 tribes)' is incorrect because it reflects a common misunderstanding of the tearing action/imagery, possibly thinking a single large piece represents all, but the Scripture clearly states only 10 out of 12 tribes are given.
options: Eleven pieces (11 tribes)
Twelve pieces (2 tribes)
One piece (all 12 tribes)
Ten pieces (10 tribes)

content: What did the man of God from Judah prophesy about the altar at Bethel?
explanation: 1 Kings 13:2 — 'O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places.'
options: The altar will stand forever
The altar would become a place of true worship
A descendant of David named Josiah will sacrifice the priests on it
The altar would fly away

content: Where did Rehoboam, son of Solomon, reign as king?
explanation:
The correct answer is 'Jerusalem (reigned over Judah)' because 1 Kings 14:21 records: 'Rehoboam son of Solomon was king in Judah... His mother's name was Naamah; she was an Ammonite. He reigned for seventeen years in Jerusalem.'

Incorrect answers: (1) 'Shechem (reigned over Israel)' - this is where Jeroboam reigned (1 Kings 12:25), but the question is about Rehoboam. (2) 'Jerusalem (reigned over Israel)' - incorrect in the scope of rule; Rehoboam reigned over Judah in Jerusalem, not Israel. (3) 'Bethel (reigned over Judah)' - Bethel was a city in Israel under Jeroboam, not where Rehoboam reigned over Judah.
options: Shechem (reigned over Israel)
Jerusalem (reigned over Israel)
Bethel (reigned over Judah)
Jerusalem (over Judah)

content: Whom did King Ahab have killed to seize his vineyard?
explanation: The correct answer is 'Naboth the Jezreelite' because the Bible clearly states in 1 Kings 21:13 that Naboth was stoned to death by the people as part of Jezebel's scheme. The distractor 'A wealthy man in the city' is close but misses key details: Naboth was a vineyard owner, not described as 'wealthy,' and his primary identifier is 'the Jezreelite.' The distractor 'Hezekiah, king of Judah' is incorrect because he is a different king, unrelated to this story. The distractor 'Naboth's wife' is out of scope since in the referenced Scripture passage, only Naboth is killed, and his wife is not mentioned.
options: A wealthy man in the city
Naboth the Jezreelite
Hezekiah, king of Judah
Naboth's wife

content: When David was old and feeble, who exalted himself and said he would be king, preparing chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him?
options: Adonijah
Absalom
Solomon
Amnon
explanation: According to 1 Kings 1:5, 'Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king,"' and prepared for himself chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. 'Absalom' was another son of David who had also rebelled but had already died before this point (true_but_off). 'Solomon' was the one God chose to succeed to the throne — he was not the one who exalted himself (wrong_detail). 'Amnon' was David's firstborn but had been killed and is unrelated to this passage (wrong_scope).

content: To attend and warm King David in his old age, his servants sought and found a beautiful young woman — what was her name?
options: Abishag
Abigail
Bathsheba
Abital
explanation: According to 1 Kings 1:3-4, they searched throughout all Israel for a beautiful young woman, found 'Abishag the Shunammite,' and brought her to the king to attend and warm him. 'Abigail' was one of David's wives but is not this person (near_passage). 'Bathsheba' was the mother of Solomon, who appears in the same chapter but in a different role (near_passage). 'Abital' was another of David's wives and is unrelated to this passage (wrong_detail).

content: Where did Solomon offer a thousand burnt offerings, and at that very place did the LORD appear to him in a dream by night?
options: Gibeon
Shiloh
Hebron
Bethel
explanation: According to 1 Kings 3:4-5, the king went to 'Gibeon' to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place, and offered a thousand burnt offerings; at Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night. 'Shiloh' was where the tabernacle had been placed during the time of the judges — it is not this location (common_misconception). 'Hebron' was where David first became king and has no connection to this dream (wrong_scope). 'Bethel' was another worship site that appears later in the narrative and does not belong to this passage (wrong_detail).

content: Two women came before Solomon requesting his judgment in a famous case — what were they disputing over?
options: A living child
An inherited field
A straying flock
An unpaid debt
explanation: According to 1 Kings 3:16-22, two women had both given birth; one child died in the night, and both claimed the living child as their own, asking the king to decide the matter. 'An inherited field' is a different type of legal dispute under the law and is not this case (wrong_detail). 'A straying flock' is completely unrelated to this story (wrong_scope). 'An unpaid debt' is also not the subject of this dispute (wrong_detail).

content: When Adonijah proclaimed himself king, how did the prophet Nathan act to ensure Solomon's succession?
options: He devised a plan for Bathsheba to go in and inform David, then entered himself afterward to confirm her account
He directly anointed Solomon before reporting the matter to David
He went to rebuke Adonijah and ordered the coronation feast to be disbanded
He convened the elders of Israel to hold a vote to select the king
explanation: According to 1 Kings 1:11-14, Nathan instructed Bathsheba to go in and remind David of his oath to make Solomon king; then 'while she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet also came in' (vv. 22-23) to confirm her words. This answer matches the precise sequence described in the text. 'Directly anointing Solomon before reporting to David' reverses the order: David gave the command first, and the anointing by Zadok and Nathan came afterward (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Going to rebuke Adonijah and dismiss the feast' never happened — Nathan did not confront Adonijah directly (wrong_detail). 'Convening the elders to vote' reflects a modern concept entirely absent from the text (common_misconception).

content: When Joab heard of Solomon's dealings with his rivals, where did Joab flee hoping to find safety?
options: To the tent of the LORD and grasped the horns of the altar
To the city of refuge Hebron under the Mosaic law
Down to Edom to take refuge with its king
Into the cave at En-gedi as David had once done
explanation: According to 1 Kings 2:28, 'Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar,' but Benaiah still killed him there on the king's orders. 'The city of refuge Hebron' was a real institution in Mosaic law, but it applied to unintentional killers—it was not where Joab fled (almost-right, true_but_off). 'Going down to Edom' is what Hadad did in a later chapter, not Joab (near_passage). 'The cave at En-gedi' is associated with David fleeing Saul and has nothing to do with Joab (wrong_scope).

content: In his final charge to Solomon, how did David instruct his son to deal with Shimei, the man who had cursed him?
options: Wisely bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol
Pardon him completely because David had sworn never to kill him
Banish him from Jerusalem for the rest of his life
Set him over the royal treasury so he could atone for his past offense
explanation: According to 1 Kings 2:8-9, David recalled that Shimei had cursed him, then charged Solomon: 'Now therefore do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol.' 'Pardon him completely because he had sworn not to kill him' is only half true: David did swear (2 Samuel 19:23) but still instructed Solomon not to spare him (almost-right, true_but_off). 'Banish him from Jerusalem for the rest of his days' was not David's charge; Shimei was merely forbidden from leaving Jerusalem—a restriction Solomon himself imposed later (wrong_detail). 'Set him over the treasury to atone for his offense' is entirely absent from the text (wrong_scope).

content: Because Solomon asked for wisdom rather than other things, God was pleased and promised to give him what he had not asked for. What was it?
options: Riches and honor surpassing all kings of his time
A life free from illness into old age
Dominion over all peoples to the ends of the earth
An unconditional and perpetual royal dynasty
explanation: According to 1 Kings 3:11-13, God commended Solomon for not asking for long life, riches, or the death of his enemies, and so granted him wisdom and also 'both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days.' 'A life free from illness' is one of the things Solomon did not ask for (long life), but God mentioned it as something Solomon had not requested—not as something unconditionally promised (almost-right, true_but_off). 'Dominion over all peoples to the ends of the earth' goes beyond the scope of the actual promise (wrong_scope). 'An unconditional perpetual dynasty' is wrong because even in v.14 the promise of long life is still conditional on obedience (wrong_detail).

content: When Adonijah used Bathsheba to ask that he be given Abishag the Shunammite in marriage, why did Solomon react in fury and order his execution?
options: The king saw the request as a bid for the throne, since Abishag belonged to his father's harem
Because the law absolutely forbade marrying a young woman who had served a deceased king
Because Abishag had been promised to Solomon, so Adonijah was violating the king's rights
Because Adonijah approached through Bathsheba rather than coming directly to the king, which was presumptuous
explanation: According to 1 Kings 2:22, Solomon replied: 'And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother,' showing the king understood that claiming a woman from his father's harem was a symbolic step toward seizing the throne (cf. 2 Samuel 16:21-22). This question demands analysis of political motive, not just surface reading. 'The law absolutely forbids it' sounds plausible but the text cites no such legal prohibition; the reason is entirely political (almost-right, common_misconception). 'Abishag had been promised to Solomon' is an invented detail; the text says only that she had served David, not that she had become his wife or been promised to anyone (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Because he went through Bathsheba instead of coming himself' misreads the emphasis: the king received Bathsheba with honor; his anger arose from the content of the request, not the manner of asking (true_but_off).

content: In the dispute over the baby, on what basis did Solomon's proposal to divide the child reveal who the true mother was?
options: The true mother pleaded to spare the child and give him up out of compassion, while the other woman agreed to divide him
The true mother immediately recognized her child's cry among the two babies
The true mother took hold of the baby first, proving her rightful claim
The true mother presented evidence of birth marks to identify her child
explanation: According to 1 Kings 3:26-27, when the king ordered the child divided, 'the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death."' The other woman said, 'He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him.' The king then ruled that the child belonged to the one willing to give him up, for she was his true mother. This question requires analyzing the logic of the test. 'Recognizing the child's cry' is an invented detail not found in the text (almost-right, common_misconception). 'Taking hold of the baby first' also did not occur; the test hinged entirely on the women's reactions to the order to divide the child (wrong_detail). 'Presenting evidence of birth marks' reflects modern forensic thinking, not the method Solomon employed (wrong_scope).

content: To provide food for King Solomon and his royal household, the king appointed twelve officials, each responsible for what period of the year?
options: Each was responsible for one month of the year
Each was responsible for one week of the year
Each was responsible for one season of the year
Each was responsible for one day of the week
explanation: According to 1 Kings 4:7, Solomon had twelve officials over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household, each responsible for one month of the year. 'One week of the year' uses the wrong unit of time and does not match the number twelve (wrong_detail). 'One season of the year' would divide the year among only four people, not twelve (wrong_detail). 'One day of the week' shifts to a different unit entirely and has no connection to the number twelve (wrong_scope).

content: When Solomon came to the throne, which foreign king sent his servants to him, because that king had always loved David all his life?
options: Hiram, king of Tyre
Pharaoh, king of Egypt
Hadad, king of Edom
Ben-hadad, king of Syria
explanation: According to 1 Kings 5:1, Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon, because Hiram had always loved David. 'Pharaoh, king of Egypt' was connected to Solomon through marriage (4:1) but was not the one who sent envoys in this passage (near_passage). 'Hadad, king of Edom' was an adversary who rose up later and was not a friend of David (wrong_scope). 'Ben-hadad, king of Syria' appears in the reigns of later kings and is outside this context entirely (wrong_scope).

content: During the construction of the temple, how were the materials prepared so that no sound of hammer, ax, or any iron tool was heard at the building site?
options: The stones were dressed at the quarry before being brought to the site
The stones were ground with sand so that they made no sound
The workers only labored at night when it was quiet
The materials were entirely wood, so no chiseling was needed
explanation: According to 1 Kings 6:7, the temple was built with stone dressed at the quarry, so that no sound of hammer, ax, or any iron tool was heard at the building site. 'Ground with sand so they made no sound' is a fabricated explanation; the text states the stones were dressed elsewhere before arrival (common_misconception). 'Workers only labored at night' is not mentioned in the text and contradicts the actual reason given (wrong_detail). 'Entirely wood' is incorrect because the temple used stone for its main walls and foundation (wrong_detail).

content: The text dates the beginning of Solomon's temple construction by counting the years since which historical event in Israel's history?
options: From the time the people of Israel came out of Egypt
From the time David became king at Hebron
From the time the people crossed the Jordan River
From the time the ark of the covenant was brought to Jerusalem
explanation: According to 1 Kings 6:1, construction began in the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign. 'From the time David became king' is a different historical marker, not the one the text uses (wrong_detail). 'From the time the people crossed the Jordan River' is close to the exodus narrative but is not the reference point given (near_passage). 'The ark of the covenant being brought to Jerusalem' happened in David's time and is not used as a chronological anchor here (wrong_scope).

content: What does the daily consumption of large quantities of fine flour, cattle, sheep, and game by Solomon's royal household reveal about his kingdom during this period?
options: The prosperity and vast scale of the royal court
A famine that required urgent stockpiling of food
Preparations for an imminent war
Extravagance that immediately provoked the people to revolt
explanation: 1 Kings 4:22-23 catalogues Solomon's enormous daily provisions, illustrating the wealth and grandeur of the royal court during a time of peaceful prosperity. 'A famine requiring stockpiling' reverses the passage's meaning: this abundance is a sign of plenty, not scarcity (common_misconception). 'Preparations for war' is incorrect because the chapter explicitly emphasizes peace on all sides (4:24-25) (wrong_detail). 'Extravagance that immediately provoked revolt' is almost-right in that the burden on the people was real in later chapters, but this passage has not yet introduced any revolt (true_but_off).

content: Solomon levied thirty thousand men as forced laborers to cut timber in Lebanon. Why did they rotate one month in Lebanon and then two months at home?
options: To distribute the work evenly and allow the men to rest at home
Because the road to Lebanon was so far that each trip took three months
Because the people of Lebanon only permitted one month of work per group
Because every three months an outbreak of disease required a temporary halt
explanation: According to 1 Kings 5:13-14, ten thousand men went to Lebanon each month and then spent two months at home, under the oversight of Adoniram, in order to rotate the workforce evenly and allow the people to rest in their hometowns. 'The road was too far, taking three months per trip' is an almost-right detail because there was indeed a three-month cycle, but the text says this was a rotation schedule, not travel time (wrong_detail). 'The people of Lebanon only allowed one month per group' fabricates a condition not found in the text (common_misconception). 'Every three months there was an outbreak of disease' is not mentioned at all (wrong_scope).

content: While the temple was being built, God promised to dwell among the people of Israel and not forsake them. What condition was this promise attached to?
options: Solomon walking in His statutes and keeping His commandments
The temple being completed within seven years
The people offering burnt offerings every day without interruption
The king personally serving as priest at the temple
explanation: According to 1 Kings 6:12-13, God promised to dwell among the people and not forsake them if Solomon would walk in His statutes, keep His commandments, and obey His rules. 'Completed within seven years' is an almost-right detail because the temple was indeed built in seven years (6:38), but this was not the stated condition of the promise (true_but_off). 'Offering burnt offerings every day' is not the condition given in this declaration (wrong_detail). 'The king serving as priest' contradicts the law, as the king was not permitted to hold the priestly office (common_misconception).

content: Solomon's wisdom is described not only by the number of his proverbs and songs, but also by his ability to discourse about what subjects?
options: Trees, animals, birds, reptiles, and fish
Stars, the sun, the moon, and the heavens
The history and genealogies of neighboring peoples
The law and the sacrificial rituals of the temple
explanation: According to 1 Kings 4:32-33, Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, composed one thousand and five songs, and discoursed about trees — from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop — as well as animals, birds, reptiles, and fish. 'Stars and the heavens' is a domain not listed in the text and is easily confused with general images of wisdom (common_misconception). 'History and genealogies of peoples' does not appear in the text's list (wrong_detail). 'Law and sacrificial rituals' is an almost-right detail because it is close to the king's broader role, but this passage emphasizes knowledge of the natural world (true_but_off).

content: Analyze the agreement between Solomon and Hiram: which party supplied what, and how was payment arranged in this deal?
options: Hiram supplied cedar and cypress timber; Solomon paid with wheat and oil for Hiram's household
Hiram supplied stonecutters; Solomon paid with gold and silver from the temple treasury
Solomon supplied cedar timber; Hiram paid with wheat and wine for the people of Israel
Hiram supplied timber and stone; Solomon paid by ceding twenty cities in Galilee
explanation: According to 1 Kings 5:6-9, Hiram arranged the felling and transport of cedar and cypress timber from Lebanon by sea, while Solomon provided food supplies — wheat and oil — for Hiram's household. 'Hiram supplied stonecutters, paid with gold and silver' reverses both the type of goods and the method of payment: the text describes timber exchanged for food, not stone for metal (wrong_detail). 'Solomon supplied timber, Hiram paid with wheat' is almost-right because it simply reverses the roles of the two parties (wrong_detail). 'Paid by ceding twenty cities in Galilee' is almost-right because the transfer of cities did occur but happened later (9:11), and is separate from this food-payment arrangement (true_but_off).

content: Compare the two cherubim placed in the Most Holy Place: how are their size, material, and wing arrangement described?
options: Two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits tall, with wings spread so that the inner wingtips touched each other in the middle and the outer wingtips touched the walls on either side
Two cherubim of pure gold, five cubits tall, with wings folded to embrace the ark
Two cherubim of bronze, ten cubits tall, with wings pointing downward to cover the mercy seat
Two cherubim of cedar wood, five cubits tall, with wings crossed above the temple door
explanation: According to 1 Kings 6:23-28, the two cherubim in the Most Holy Place were made of olive wood, each statue ten cubits tall with each wing five cubits long. Their wings were spread so that the inner wingtips touched each other at the center of the room and the outer wingtips touched the two walls; the figures were then overlaid with gold. 'Pure gold, five cubits tall, wings folded embracing the ark' confuses these large wooden statues with the cherubim on the mercy seat made in Moses' time (common_misconception). 'Bronze, wings pointing down to cover the mercy seat' has the wrong material and conflates this passage with imagery from Exodus (wrong_scope). 'Cedar wood, five cubits tall, wings crossed above the door' is almost-right in appearance but gets the material, height, and wing position all wrong (wrong_detail).
tags: Cherubim in the Most Holy Place

content: How many years did Solomon spend building his own palace?
options: Seven years
Thirteen years
Twenty years
Forty years
explanation: According to 1 Kings 7:1, 'Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house.' 'Seven years' was the time spent building the temple of the LORD, not the palace (near_passage, 1 Kings 6:38). 'Twenty years' is the combined total time for building both the temple and the palace together (wrong_detail, 1 Kings 9:10). 'Forty years' is the length of Solomon's reign and is unrelated to the construction of the palace (wrong_scope).

content: What was the name of the skilled craftsman whom Solomon brought from Tyre to do the bronze work for the temple?
options: Hiram
Bezalel
Oholiab
Adoniram
explanation: According to 1 Kings 7:13–14, the king sent and brought Hiram from Tyre; he was a craftsman in bronze, full of wisdom, understanding, and skill. 'Bezalel' and 'Oholiab' were craftsmen in Moses' time who built the tabernacle, not craftsmen of Solomon's era (wrong_scope, Exodus 31). 'Adoniram' was in charge of the forced labor, not a bronze craftsman (wrong_detail, 1 Kings 4:6).

content: What did the bronze 'Sea' that Hiram cast for the temple rest on?
options: Twelve bronze oxen facing four directions
Four bronze pillars five cubits high
A square stone pedestal carved with cherubim
Ten bronze stands with wheels
explanation: According to 1 Kings 7:25, the Sea stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The answer 'ten bronze stands with wheels' is almost correct, since those were indeed objects Hiram cast in the same passage, but they supported the smaller basins rather than the Sea (near_passage, 1 Kings 7:27–30). 'Four bronze pillars' is confused with the two pillars Jachin and Boaz set at the entrance porch, which did not support the Sea (wrong_detail, 1 Kings 7:21). 'A square stone pedestal carved with cherubim' is never described in connection with the Sea; the cherubim belonged to the Most Holy Place (wrong_scope).

content: Hiram set up two bronze pillars at the entrance porch of the temple and gave them names. Why were these two pillars given individual names?
options: Because their names carry theological meaning about establishment and strength in God
Because they supported the entire roof above the Most Holy Place in the temple
Because they were used to hang lamps that illuminated the entire temple
Because they marked the spot where the priests stood to offer daily sacrifices
explanation: According to 1 Kings 7:21, the pillar on the right was named Jachin (meaning 'He establishes') and the pillar on the left was named Boaz (meaning 'In him is strength'); the names carry theological meaning about establishment and strength in God. 'Supporting the entire roof of the Most Holy Place' is almost correct in that the two pillars were indeed set at the entrance porch, but the text does not say they supported the roof of the Most Holy Place (wrong_detail). 'Hanging lamps' is confused with the golden lampstands inside the temple (wrong_scope, 1 Kings 7:49). 'Marking the spot where the priests stood to offer daily sacrifices' is not a reason given in the text (common_misconception).

content: At the dedication of the temple, which sacred object did the priests carry in and place in the Most Holy Place?
options: The ark of the covenant of the LORD
The golden altar of incense
The seven-branched golden lampstand
The large bronze Sea
explanation: According to 1 Kings 8:6, the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD into the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim. 'The altar of incense' and 'the golden lampstand' were furnishings of the Holy Place and were not carried into the Most Holy Place (wrong_scope, 1 Kings 7:48–49). 'The large bronze Sea' was placed in the courtyard for the priests to wash and did not go inside the temple proper (wrong_detail, 1 Kings 7:39).

content: At the dedication of the temple, what was inside the ark of the covenant?
options: The two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb
The staff of Aaron that had budded
A jar of manna preserved from the wilderness
The scroll of the law written by Moses
explanation: According to 1 Kings 8:9, there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses had placed there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel. 'Aaron's staff that budded' and 'the jar of manna' are almost-right because these items were once associated with the ark according to Hebrews 9:4, but verse 8:9 emphasizes that at this point only the two stone tablets remained (common_misconception). 'The scroll of the law' was placed beside the ark, not inside it (wrong_detail, Deut. 31:26).
tags: Contents of the Ark of the Covenant

content: Why could the priests not continue standing to minister after bringing the ark into the temple?
options: Because the cloud of the LORD's glory filled the temple so that they could not stand to minister
Because darkness suddenly fell, forcing them to stop the ceremony midway
Because the king commanded the priests to withdraw so that the people could enter
Because fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering on the altar
explanation: According to 1 Kings 8:10–11, when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the glory of the LORD filling the temple. 'Fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering' is almost-right because that is a similar event recorded in 2 Chronicles 7:1, but it is not the reason stated in 1 Kings 8 (near_passage). 'Darkness suddenly fell' is never mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). 'The king commanded the priests to withdraw so that the people could enter' is a fabricated detail that contradicts the actual events (common_misconception).

content: What posture did Solomon assume when he began the dedicatory prayer for the temple?
options: He stood before the altar and spread out his hands toward heaven
He prostrated himself on the ground before the ark of the covenant
He sat on his throne in the midst of the assembly
He knelt on a bronze platform
explanation: According to 1 Kings 8:22, Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven in prayer. 'Kneeling on a bronze platform' is almost-right because that detail comes from the parallel account in 2 Chronicles 6:13, but 1 Kings 8:22 records that he was 'standing' (near_passage). 'Prostrating himself on the ground' is not the posture mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). 'Sitting on his throne' contradicts the text since he was standing in prayer (wrong_scope).

content: In his prayer, what paradoxical recognition did Solomon express about the relationship between God and the temple he had just built?
options: The temple was spacious enough to contain God's presence forever
Even the highest heavens cannot contain God, let alone this temple
God would only dwell in the temple when the people brought offerings
The temple was more precious than the heavens because it held the ark of the covenant
explanation: According to 1 Kings 8:27, Solomon said: 'Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!' — this is the paradox: he had just built the temple yet acknowledged that the infinite God cannot be contained. 'The temple is spacious enough to contain God forever' is the direct opposite of what he said (common_misconception). 'God would only dwell when the people bring offerings' is almost-right because the prayer does mention offerings in other verses, but verse 27 does not condition God's presence on that requirement (wrong_detail). 'The temple is more precious than the heavens' is almost-right because it subtly inverts the comparison in verse 27 — in reality, if even the heavens cannot contain God, the temple is all the more insufficient (wrong_scope).

content: When praying about 'the foreigner' from a distant land who turns toward the temple and prays, what did Solomon ask God to do, and what vision of the temple does this reveal?
options: Answer the foreigner's prayer so that all peoples of the earth would know and fear God's name
Answer only if the foreigner submits to circumcision according to the law
Drive the foreigner away from the holy land to keep the temple pure
Bless the foreigner but keep God's name hidden from them
explanation: According to 1 Kings 8:43, Solomon asked God to hear from heaven the foreigner's prayer, 'in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel' — revealing a missionary vision in which the temple is a place toward which all nations turn. 'Answer only if the foreigner submits to circumcision' is almost-right because circumcision was a genuine covenant sign, but the prayer places no such condition on the foreigner (common_misconception). 'Drive the foreigner away to keep the temple pure' is the complete opposite of the welcoming spirit of verses 41–43 (wrong_scope). 'Bless the foreigner but keep God's name hidden from them' is almost-right because it inverts the very purpose — the main goal is precisely that God's name would become known to all peoples (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 9, the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time. Where had He previously appeared to him?
options: At Gibeon
At Hebron
At Shiloh
At Bethel
explanation: 1 Kings 9:2 records that the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, 'as he had appeared to him at Gibeon' (see 3:5). Hebron is where David was anointed king, not where God appeared to Solomon (wrong_detail). Shiloh is where the tabernacle was placed during the time of the judges, unrelated to this vision (wrong_scope). Bethel is associated with Jacob and later with Jeroboam's altar, not where He appeared to Solomon (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 9, how many years did it take Solomon to complete both projects — the house of the LORD and the king's palace?
options: Twenty years
Seven years
Thirteen years
Forty years
explanation: 1 Kings 9:10 records: 'At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house.' Seven years was the time to build the temple alone (6:38), not both projects (wrong_detail). Thirteen years was the time to build the king's palace alone (7:1), also only a portion, not the combined total (wrong_detail). Forty years was the full length of Solomon's reign, not the time spent in construction (true_but_off).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 9, Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, near Elath. On the shore of which sea was this fleet located?
options: The Red Sea
The Great Sea (the Mediterranean)
The Sea of Kinnereth
The Dead Sea
explanation: 1 Kings 9:26 records: 'King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.' The Great Sea (the Mediterranean) lies to the west and is not where this fleet was stationed (wrong_detail). The Sea of Kinnereth (the Sea of Galilee) is deep inland to the north with no passage to Ophir (wrong_scope). The Dead Sea has no harbor opening to the open ocean for maritime trade (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 10, in what unit was the gold Solomon received in a single year measured?
options: Talents
Shekels
Bekas
Gerahs
explanation: 1 Kings 10:14 records: 'Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold' — talents being the large unit used for bulk tribute gold. A shekel is a far smaller unit suited to everyday transactions, not annual treasury totals (wrong_detail). A beka is only half a shekel, making it even smaller (wrong_detail). A gerah is the smallest unit in the Hebrew weight system and would never be used to quantify a royal treasury (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 9, why did King Hiram name the region of twenty cities that Solomon gave him 'the land of Cabul'?
options: Because when he came to inspect them, he was not pleased with those cities
Because it was the homeland of his ancestors
Because he wanted to honor his friendship with Solomon
Because the cities were richer than he had expected
explanation: 1 Kings 9:12–13 records that Hiram came to inspect the cities Solomon had given him, 'but they did not please him,' so he said, 'What are these cities that you have given me, my brother?' and called the region Cabul, implying he considered them worthless (wrong_detail ruled out). 'Homeland of his ancestors' is an invented detail; the text states plainly that his dissatisfaction was the reason for the name (wrong_detail). 'To honor the friendship' reverses the meaning entirely: the name carries a tone of disappointment and reproach, not tribute (common_misconception). 'Richer than expected' directly contradicts the text, since Hiram disparaged the cities (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 9, Solomon subjected the remaining peoples — such as the Amorites, Hittites, and Perizzites — to forced labor. However, which group did he NOT make slaves?
options: The people of Israel
The Jebusites
The Hivites
The Girgashites
explanation: 1 Kings 9:22 states: 'But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves,' for they were his soldiers, officials, and commanders. Verses 20–21 list the Jebusites among the peoples subjected to forced labor, so that option is incorrect (near_passage). The Hivites also belonged to the remaining foreign peoples forced into compulsory labor and were not exempt (near_passage). The Girgashites likewise were among the remaining Canaanite peoples subjected to forced service and were not exempt (near_passage).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 10, after the queen of Sheba witnessed all of Solomon's wisdom, his palace, his food, and his burnt offerings, what was her reaction?
options: She was overwhelmed to the point that there was no more spirit in her
She disguised herself and quietly slipped away that very night
She was furious because she felt he had been greatly exaggerated by rumor
She demanded that Solomon give her half of his entire kingdom
explanation: 1 Kings 10:5 records that after seeing everything, 'there was no more breath in her' — the text conveys that she was utterly overwhelmed and breathless with awe. 'Disguising herself and leaving in the night' is a fabricated detail absent from the account of the grand reception (wrong_detail). 'Being furious because of exaggerated rumors' reverses the meaning: she acknowledged that reality surpassed the report (v. 7), rather than being angry (common_misconception). 'Demanding half the kingdom' confuses this episode with another scriptural detail and does not belong to this encounter (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 10, the great ivory throne Solomon made had six steps. What figures decorated each side of every step?
options: Twelve lions, two standing on either side of each step
Twelve bronze bulls, two on either side of each step
Two golden cherubim with outstretched wings overshadowing the throne
Twelve finely carved palm trees, two on either side of each step
explanation: 1 Kings 10:19–20 records that the throne had six steps with 'twelve lions standing there, one on each end of a step on the six steps,' two lions per step. The twelve bronze bulls belong to the 'molten sea' in the temple (7:25), not to the throne (near_passage). The two cherubim with outstretched wings are imagery associated with the Most Holy Place and the ark of the covenant, not the throne's decoration (near_passage). Twelve carved palm trees belonged to the decorations on the temple walls, not the steps of the throne (near_passage).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 10, all of Solomon's drinking vessels were gold and 'none were of silver.' What reason does the text give for why silver was considered of little value in his day?
options: Because silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon
Because the law forbade the use of silver in the king's palace
Because vassal nations would only pay tribute in gold
Because all the silver had been used up in building the temple
explanation: 1 Kings 10:21 gives the text's own reason: all the vessels were of pure gold, and none of silver, 'because silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon' — it was so abundant that it lost its value (v. 27 says silver was as common as stone). 'A law forbidding silver' is an invented regulation not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Vassal nations paying tribute only in gold' is a false inference, since verse 25 records that they brought both silver and gold, along with weapons, spices, and more (near_passage). 'All silver used up in building the temple' contradicts verse 27, which shows silver was exceedingly plentiful and by no means exhausted (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Kings chapter 9, the LORD warned that if Israel forsook him and followed other gods, what would happen, and what would the nations say when they saw the temple in ruins?
options: Israel would be cut off from the land, the temple would become a heap of ruins, and people would ask why the LORD had brought this disaster
Israel would suffer one defeat but then be restored, and the nations would praise his power
The temple would be burned but the people would remain in the land, and the nations would mock their poverty
Solomon would immediately lose his throne, and the nations would exalt other gods above the LORD
explanation: 1 Kings 9:7–9 records that the LORD would 'cut off Israel from the land,' make the temple 'a heap of ruins,' and passersby would ask why he had brought this disaster — then answer that it was because the people forsook the LORD and worshiped other gods. The option of 'one defeat followed by restoration' diminishes the severity of the punishment and reverses the nations' reaction into praise, contrary to the text, which says they would be appalled at the calamity (wrong_detail). The option of 'people remaining in the land' directly contradicts the declaration of being cut off from the land, even though the destruction of the temple is correctly reflected (wrong_detail). The option of 'Solomon immediately losing his throne' confuses this warning with the separate word concerning the tearing away of the kingdom during the reign of his son in chapter 11, which is outside this passage's scope (wrong_scope).

content: God raised up an adversary from Edom against Solomon. What was this Edomite's name?
options: Hadad
Rezon
Jeroboam
Hadadezer
explanation: According to 1 Kings 11:14, the LORD raised up Hadad the Edomite, of the royal house of Edom, as an adversary against Solomon. Rezon was also an adversary raised up by God, but he was a Syrian from Damascus, not an Edomite (wrong_detail). Jeroboam was an opponent, but he was an Israelite from the tribe of Ephraim, not an Edomite (wrong_scope). Hadadezer was the king of Zobah during the time of David and has no connection to this chapter (near_passage).

content: After the ten northern tribes broke away from the house of David, whom did they make king over them?
options: Jeroboam
Rehoboam
Adonijah
Ahijah
explanation: According to 1 Kings 12:20, when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him and made him king over all Israel. Rehoboam was Solomon's son, who continued to reign only over the tribe of Judah, not the ten northern tribes (wrong_detail). Adonijah was David's son who had previously attempted to seize the throne before Solomon's time and is not relevant here (near_passage). Ahijah was the prophet who foretold the division of the kingdom; he was not the king who was set up (wrong_scope).

content: To keep the people from going to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices, Jeroboam made two golden calves and set them up at two locations. Where were these two places?
options: Bethel and Dan
Shechem and Penuel
Dan and Jerusalem
Bethel and Samaria
explanation: According to 1 Kings 12:29, Jeroboam set one golden calf at Bethel and the other at Dan. Shechem and Penuel were cities Jeroboam built or fortified (12:25) but were not the locations where the golden calves were placed (near_passage). Jerusalem was precisely the place Jeroboam wanted the people to avoid, so the calves could not have been set up there (wrong_detail). Samaria only became the capital later under Omri and did not yet exist in this context (wrong_scope).

content: The text records that Solomon had an extraordinarily large number of wives and concubines. According to the account, how many wives (princesses) and how many concubines did he have?
options: 700 wives and 300 concubines
300 wives and 700 concubines
1,000 wives and 300 concubines
700 wives and 700 concubines
explanation: According to 1 Kings 11:3, Solomon had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines, and his wives turned his heart away. The option reversing these to 300 wives and 700 concubines simply swaps the two figures (wrong_detail). The figure of 1,000 wives inflates the total into the wives column (wrong_detail). The figure of 700 and 700 repeats the wrong number for the concubines (wrong_detail).

content: When the people asked Rehoboam to lighten their heavy yoke, why did he ultimately answer harshly and say he would make their yoke even heavier?
options: Because he rejected the counsel of the elders and listened instead to the young men who had grown up with him
Because the elders advised him to be firm in order to maintain his authority
Because the prophet Ahijah had told him to make the people's yoke heavier
Because his father Solomon had charged him to increase the tax burden
explanation: According to 1 Kings 12:8–11, Rehoboam rejected the counsel of the elders — who advised him to speak kindly to the people so that they would serve him always — and instead followed the advice of the young men who had grown up with him, and so he answered the people harshly. The option claiming the elders advised him to be firm reverses the actual content of their counsel, which was gentle and conciliatory (wrong_detail). Ahijah was the prophet who foretold the division of the kingdom to Jeroboam; he did not advise Rehoboam on taxes (wrong_scope). Attributing this to a dying charge from Solomon is a fabricated detail — the text records no such thing (common_misconception).

content: What does Solomon's building of shrines for foreign gods reveal about his heart compared to his father David?
options: His heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father
He completely rejected the LORD and worshiped only foreign gods
He only permitted foreigners to worship their own gods but remained wholly devoted himself
He built the shrines solely to please his allied vassal kings
explanation: According to 1 Kings 11:4, when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. The option saying he completely rejected the LORD is an overstatement, since the text emphasizes that his heart was not wholly true rather than a total abandonment (wrong_detail). The option saying he remained wholly devoted directly contradicts verse 4 (common_misconception). The reason of pleasing allied vassal kings is a detail absent from the text, which attributes the cause to his foreign wives (wrong_scope).

content: When pronouncing judgment to tear the kingdom from Solomon's hand, why did God decide to leave one tribe for his descendants?
options: For the sake of David and for the sake of Jerusalem which He had chosen
For the sake of Solomon's own righteousness during the early years of his reign
For the sake of the oath He had made with Abraham concerning his descendants
Because the people of Judah were more faithful than the northern tribes
explanation: According to 1 Kings 11:13, God said He would leave one tribe for the sake of David His servant and for the sake of Jerusalem which He had chosen. The reason about Solomon's righteousness is wrong, since the entire passage condemns him for sin rather than commending him (wrong_detail). The oath with Abraham is a real covenant but is not the reason cited here — the covenant in view is the one with David (true_but_off). The claim that the people of Judah were more faithful is an inference not found in the text; the reason given is for the sake of David and Jerusalem (common_misconception).

content: When Rehoboam assembled the armies of Judah and Benjamin to fight against the house of Israel to recover the kingdom, why did they disband and return home?
options: Because the prophet Shemaiah delivered God's word forbidding them to fight against their brothers
Because Jeroboam proactively sued for peace and paid tribute to Rehoboam
Because Judah's army was too small compared to the ten tribes and did not dare to fight
Because the prophet Ahijah appeared and prevented the war between the two regions
explanation: According to 1 Kings 12:22–24, the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God, commanding them not to go and fight against their brothers the people of Israel, for this thing was from Him; so they listened to the word of the LORD and returned home. The option saying Jeroboam sued for peace and paid tribute is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). The reason of having too few troops is incorrect, since verse 21 states that Rehoboam assembled 180,000 chosen warriors (wrong_detail). Ahijah was Jeroboam's prophet in the previous chapter; the one who delivered the command against war here was Shemaiah (near_passage).

content: Comparing the circumstances that caused Jeroboam to flee to Egypt with what the prophet Ahijah had promised him, what do we observe?
options: Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam after the prophecy, so he fled and took refuge with King Shishak of Egypt until Solomon died
Solomon appointed Jeroboam as chief overseer, so he went to Egypt to handle tribute affairs until the king died
Pharaoh seized Jeroboam as a hostage to pressure Solomon, and Ahijah promised to rescue him
Jeroboam proactively went to Egypt to enlist Shishak's army to overthrow Solomon immediately
explanation: According to 1 Kings 11:40, after Ahijah told Jeroboam he would rule over ten tribes, Solomon sought to kill him, so he fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and remained there until Solomon died. The option saying he was appointed chief overseer and went to handle tribute affairs contradicts the true reason — he fled to save his life (wrong_detail); although he had previously been appointed by Solomon to oversee the forced labor of the house of Joseph (11:28), that was not the reason he went to Egypt (near_passage). The option about being seized as a hostage is entirely fabricated (common_misconception). The option saying he enlisted Shishak to overthrow Solomon immediately is wrong about the timing, since he only sheltered there until Solomon died before returning (wrong_detail).

content: Analyzing the religious measures Jeroboam established, what was the key motivation behind all these changes?
options: Fear that if the people went up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices, their hearts would turn back to Rehoboam and they would kill him
A desire to restore the ancient form of worship practiced by the patriarchs before Solomon's temple
Obedience to a direct command from God through the prophet Shemaiah about a new place of worship
Imitation of the worship rituals of King Shishak of Egypt, where he had previously taken refuge
explanation: According to 1 Kings 12:26–27, Jeroboam said in his heart that if the people continued to go up to offer sacrifices at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, the heart of this people would turn back to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they would kill him and return to Rehoboam; therefore he set up golden calves, shrines at the high places, and a special feast. The option about restoring ancient worship is a false justification, since the text calls this sin something Jeroboam devised on his own (common_misconception). The option saying he obeyed God's command through Shemaiah is wrong because Shemaiah only delivered the word forbidding Judah to wage war and said nothing about establishing a new place of worship (wrong_scope). The option about imitating Shishak is an inference not found in the text; the stated motivation is plainly his fear of losing power and his life (wrong_detail).

content: When King Jeroboam stretched out his hand and ordered the arrest of the man of God at the altar in Bethel, what happened to the king's hand?
options: The king's hand withered and he could not draw it back
The king's hand broke immediately
The king's hand was bitten by a snake
The king's hand bled without stopping
explanation: According to 1 Kings 13:4, when the king stretched out his hand against the man of God and said, 'Seize him!' his 'hand which he stretched out against him dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself.' The correct answer is 'The king's hand withered and he could not draw it back.' (1) 'Broke immediately' is an incorrect detail — the text says it withered, not broke (wrong_detail). (2) 'Was bitten by a snake' is an invented detail not found in the passage (wrong_detail). (3) 'Bled without stopping' is also an incorrect detail not present in the text (wrong_detail).

content: On the way home after eating bread in disobedience to God's command, what animal killed the man of God from Judah?
options: A bear
A wolf
A lion
A leopard
explanation: According to 1 Kings 13:24, as the man of God was traveling, 'a lion met him on the road and killed him.' The correct answer is 'A lion.' (1) 'A bear' is a different wild animal, not the one mentioned in the passage (wrong_detail). (2) 'A wolf' is also an incorrect detail about the animal species (wrong_detail). (3) 'A leopard' is similarly an incorrect detail (wrong_detail).

content: When his son fell ill, King Jeroboam told his wife to disguise herself and go consult which prophet about the fate of the child?
options: The prophet Samuel
The prophet Ahijah
The prophet Elijah
The prophet Nathan
explanation: According to 1 Kings 14:2, Jeroboam told his wife: 'Arise, and go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there… he will tell you what shall happen to the child.' The correct answer is 'The prophet Ahijah.' (1) 'Samuel' had already died in an earlier era — wrong scope (wrong_scope). (2) 'Elijah' belongs to a later period of the kings — wrong scope (wrong_scope). (3) 'Nathan' was a prophet in the time of David and Solomon — wrong scope (wrong_scope).

content: In the fifth year of King Rehoboam's reign, which king came up against Jerusalem and plundered the treasuries of the temple?
options: King Sennacherib of Assyria
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon
King Shishak of Egypt
King Hazael of Syria
explanation: According to 1 Kings 14:25-26, 'In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD.' The correct answer is 'King Shishak of Egypt.' (1) 'Sennacherib of Assyria' attacked Judah in a later period during Hezekiah's reign — wrong scope (wrong_scope). (2) 'Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon' destroyed Jerusalem many centuries later — wrong scope (wrong_scope). (3) 'Hazael of Syria' was a king of a different nation — incorrect detail (wrong_detail).

content: Why did the man of God from Judah ultimately turn back and eat bread, contrary to God's original command?
options: He believed the old prophet's claim that an angel had delivered a new command to him
He was too hungry and exhausted from the long journey to resist
God himself appeared and told him he was permitted to eat
King Jeroboam had persuaded him to accept the dinner invitation
explanation: According to 1 Kings 13:18-19, the old prophet from Bethel lied: 'I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, "Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water."' So the man of God returned with him and ate. The correct answer is that he believed the old prophet's claim about receiving an angelic message. (1) 'Too hungry and exhausted' is a plausible reason but is not the cause stated in the text (true_but_off). (2) 'God himself appeared and spoke' is wrong — this was the old prophet's lie, not a genuine divine command (wrong_detail, almost-right since it revolves around the same pretext of a 'new command'). (3) 'King Jeroboam persuaded him' is wrong — he had already refused the king's invitation earlier (near_passage, confused with 13:8).

content: What strange detail at the scene where the man of God died shows that this was God's judgment rather than an ordinary accident?
options: The lion stood beside the body without eating it or attacking the donkey
The lion carried the body away and left the donkey unharmed
The donkey fled and the lion chased it into the city
The lion lay dead beside the body
explanation: According to 1 Kings 13:28 (ESV), the old prophet found 'the body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.' This unnatural scene made clear that this was a deliberate judgment from God. The correct answer is 'the lion stood beside the body without eating it or attacking the donkey.' (1) 'Carried the body away' is an incorrect detail—the body remained on the road (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'The donkey fled and the lion chased it into the city' fabricates events not found in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'The lion lay dead beside the body' is wrong—the lion was still standing guard (wrong_detail, almost-right).

content: According to the prophecy of Ahijah, why was only Jeroboam's son given a proper burial while the rest of the king's house would face a shameful end?
options: Because the child was the firstborn and therefore entitled to special privilege by law
Because in the house of Jeroboam, only he had something good that pleased God
Because the child was too young to have sinned like his father
Because his mother humbled herself by disguising herself to petition the prophet
explanation: According to 1 Kings 14:13 (ESV), Ahijah said the child would be mourned and buried 'because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.' The correct answer is 'in the house of Jeroboam, only he had something good that pleased God.' (1) 'The firstborn entitled to special privilege by law' is a plausible reason but not what the text states (true_but_off). (2) 'Too young to have sinned' is a theological inference not present in the passage (common_misconception, almost-right because it still concerns the child). (3) 'Because his mother disguised herself to petition the prophet' is wrong—the disguise was exposed by God and brought no favor (near_passage, confuses 14:6).

content: After the temple was plundered of its golden shields, what did King Rehoboam do to replace them?
options: He made bronze shields to replace them
He cast new golden shields more expensive than the originals
He abolished the use of shields in ceremonies entirely
He borrowed silver shields from neighboring nations
explanation: According to 1 Kings 14:27 (ESV), 'King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.' Replacing gold with bronze illustrates Judah's decline. The correct answer is 'he made bronze shields.' (1) 'Cast new golden shields' contradicts the text—if gold remained, it would not have been plundered (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'Abolished the use of shields' is wrong—the king continued to keep and use the shields (wrong_detail). (3) 'Borrowed silver shields from neighboring nations' is an invented detail not found in the passage (wrong_detail).

content: Comparing the two 'prophets' in chapter 13: what paradox stands out when examining the fulfillment of prophecy and the fate of each man?
options: The old prophet who lied survived, and with his own mouth he proclaimed the judgment that was fulfilled upon the one who had obeyed
The man of God lied and was therefore killed, while the old prophet was truthful and therefore lived long on the earth
Both men prophesied truly and were equally rewarded by God
The old prophet proclaimed a very severe judgment, but in the end it never came to pass on anyone
explanation: According to 1 Kings 13:18-22 (ESV), the old prophet lied to deceive the man of God, but afterward the LORD spoke through him to proclaim the judgment: 'your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers'; this word was fulfilled when a lion killed the man of God (13:24). The paradox is that the one who lied survived and became the very mouthpiece for God's true word, while the one who obeyed died for a single act of disobedience. The correct answer captures this paradox. (1) 'The man of God lied and was killed' reverses the roles—it was the old prophet who lied (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'Both were equally rewarded' is wrong—one was killed (wrong_scope). (3) 'The judgment never came to pass' contradicts 13:24-26, where the word was indeed fulfilled (wrong_detail, almost-right).

content: When Jeroboam's wife disguised herself to visit Ahijah, what showed that her attempt to conceal her identity was completely futile before God?
options: Although Ahijah had gone blind from old age, as soon as he heard her footsteps he called out her exact identity: 'wife of Jeroboam'
Ahijah recognized her by seeing the royal garments she wore beneath her disguise
The son who accompanied her accidentally called her mother in front of the prophet
Ahijah demanded she remove her disguise before he would speak the prophecy
explanation: According to 1 Kings 14:4-6 (ESV), 'Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age'; yet the LORD had told him in advance, so 'when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another?"' A blind man calling out her exact identity proves that God sees through all concealment and the disguise was useless. The correct answer names the detail that he was blind yet still identified her correctly. (1) 'Recognized her by seeing her royal garments' contradicts the text—Ahijah was blind and she was in disguise, not wearing royal clothing (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'The son who accompanied her called her mother' invents a character—the sick child was at home, not present (wrong_scope, almost-right). (3) 'Demanded she remove her disguise before speaking' is wrong—he recognized her immediately and prophesied at once (wrong_detail).

content: Who was the son of Rehoboam that became king over Judah and reigned in Jerusalem?
options: Abijam
Jeroboam
Nadab
Baasha
explanation: 1 Kings 15:1-2 records that Abijam son of Rehoboam became king over Judah and reigned in Jerusalem for three years. Jeroboam was king of Israel (the northern kingdom) and was not a son of Rehoboam (wrong_scope). Nadab was the son of Jeroboam, king of Israel (wrong_scope). Baasha was the king of Israel who killed Nadab and had no connection to the line of Rehoboam (wrong_detail).

content: Which king of Judah was described as doing what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as David his ancestor had done?
options: Asa
Abijam
Baasha
Elah
