explanation: 1 Kings 15:11 records that Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his ancestor had done. Abijam committed the same sins as his father and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD (wrong_detail). Baasha was a king of Israel who did evil (wrong_scope). Elah was a king of Israel and the son of Baasha (wrong_scope).

content: Who conspired against and killed Nadab son of Jeroboam in order to seize the throne of Israel?
options: Baasha
Zimri
Omri
Tibni
explanation: 1 Kings 15:27-28 records that Baasha son of Ahijah conspired against Nadab, killed him, and reigned in his place. Zimri is the one who later killed Baasha's descendant Elah, not Nadab (near_passage). Omri was the military commander who was proclaimed king in opposition to Zimri (wrong_detail). Tibni was the one who contested the throne with Omri and had no connection to Nadab (wrong_detail).

content: Which king bought a hill and built on it a new capital city for the kingdom of Israel?
options: Omri
Baasha
Zimri
Ahab
explanation: 1 Kings 16:23-24 records that Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer, built a city on it, and named it Samaria. Baasha had his capital at Tirzah and did not build Samaria (wrong_detail). Zimri reigned only seven days before dying and built no capital (wrong_detail). Ahab was Omri's son who succeeded him and expanded Baal worship there, but he was not the one who bought the hill and built the city (near_passage).

content: When Baasha king of Israel fortified Ramah to blockade Judah, what did Asa do to force Baasha to withdraw?
options: Took silver and gold from the temple treasury and hired the king of Syria to attack northern Israel
Prayed to the LORD and then personally defeated Baasha's army
Sent envoys to negotiate peace and offer tribute directly to Baasha
Allied with Egypt to attack Israel from the south
explanation: 1 Kings 15:18-20 records that Asa took the remaining silver and gold from the treasury of the temple and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria to break his treaty with Baasha; Syria then attacked the northern cities of Israel, forcing Baasha to abandon Ramah. The option about Asa praying to the LORD and personally defeating the enemy refers to his earlier victory over the Cushites in a different chapter, not this situation (wrong_scope). Sending envoys to make peace and offer tribute to Baasha contradicts the text, since Asa leveraged outside power to pressure Baasha (wrong_detail). An alliance with Egypt is a fabricated detail; the text names Syria (common_misconception).

content: What aspect of Asa's reform is especially noteworthy regarding Maacah, the king's grandmother?
options: He removed her from the position of queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah
He elevated her to queen mother because of her loyalty to the LORD
He put her in charge of overseeing the renovation of the temple in Jerusalem
He exiled her to Syria because she had conspired with King Ben-hadad
explanation: 1 Kings 15:13 records that Asa removed Maacah his grandmother from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah; he cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron. Elevating her to queen mother is the exact opposite of what the text says — Asa deposed her (wrong_detail). Putting her in charge of the temple renovation is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_scope). Exiling her to Syria confuses this passage with Asa's later appeal to Ben-hadad, but Maacah was not exiled (near_passage).

content: Why was the entire house of Baasha destroyed when Zimri rebelled, according to the prophecy spoken beforehand?
options: Because Baasha had provoked the LORD to anger through sins like those of the house of Jeroboam
Because Baasha worshiped Baal, introduced by a foreign queen
Because Baasha plundered the silver and gold of the temple to hire the king of Syria
Because Baasha set up a golden calf in the city of Tirzah
explanation: 1 Kings 16:7, 13 records that the house of Baasha was destroyed because of all the sins that Baasha and his son Elah had committed, making Israel sin and provoking the LORD to anger with their idols — just as the house of Jeroboam had done. Worshiping Baal introduced by a foreign queen was the sin of Ahab through Jezebel, not Baasha (wrong_scope). Plundering the temple's silver and gold to hire Syria was what Asa did — wrongly attributed here to Baasha (near_passage). Setting up a golden calf was what Jeroboam did at Bethel and Dan, not Baasha at Tirzah (common_misconception).

content: When the army proclaimed Omri king and besieged Tirzah, how did Zimri meet his end?
options: He set fire to the king's palace over himself and burned to death inside it
He was captured alive by Omri and executed before the people
He drank poison in the palace when the city fell
He fled to Syria and was killed along the way
explanation: 1 Kings 16:18 records that when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over himself with fire, and died. Being captured alive and executed by Omri contradicts the text, since Zimri took his own life before he could be taken (wrong_detail). Drinking poison is a fabricated manner of death not found in Scripture (common_misconception). Fleeing to Syria conflates this event with flight narratives of other figures — Zimri stayed and burned himself alive (wrong_detail).

content: The text emphasizes that Ahab did more evil than all the kings before him. What specifically made his sin regarded as the most serious compared to his predecessors?
options: He married Jezebel and built an altar and a temple for Baal in Samaria
He continued keeping the golden calves of Jeroboam as the kings before him had done
He deposed the queen mother and erected an Asherah pole for himself
He plundered the temple's silver and gold to hire the king of Syria against a neighboring nation
explanation: 1 Kings 16:31–33 records that Ahab treated the sins of Jeroboam as a trivial matter, and went further: he married Jezebel the daughter of the king of Sidon, went and served Baal and worshiped him, erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal that he built in Samaria, and made an Asherah pole — provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger more than all the kings of Israel before him. It was the introduction of Baal worship as state religion that made his sin the gravest. Keeping the golden calves of Jeroboam is indeed a sin Ahab also committed, but it was common to all previous kings and is not what set Ahab apart (true_but_off). Deposing the queen mother and making an Asherah pole describes Asa's reform concerning Maacah — wrongly attributed here to Ahab (near_passage). Plundering the temple's silver and gold to hire Syria was what Asa did, not Ahab (wrong_scope).

content: Comparing Abijam and Asa, father and son kings of Judah, which statement correctly distinguishes the two reigns according to how the text evaluates them?
options: Abijam's heart was not wholly true to the LORD, whereas Asa removed idols and did what was right
Both did what was right, but Asa did not remove the high places
Abijam removed the idols, while Asa tolerated Baal worship
Abijam had a long and peaceful reign, while Asa was constantly at war with Israel
explanation: 1 Kings 15:3 records that Abijam walked in all the sins of his father, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father. By contrast, 15:11–13 records that Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, expelled the male cult prostitutes, removed all the idols his fathers had made, and deposed his grandmother Maacah from being queen mother. The option claiming both did what was right is wrong about Abijam, even though the detail that Asa did not remove the high places is accurate according to 15:14 (true_but_off). The option that reverses the roles — crediting Abijam with removing idols and blaming Asa for tolerating Baal worship — is directly contrary to the text (wrong_detail). The option about length of reign is wrong because Abijam reigned only three years and also faced war with Jeroboam (wrong_detail).

content: When Elijah first appeared to King Ahab to declare the word of the LORD, what did he announce would cease in the coming years?
options: There would be neither dew nor rain
Crops would be devoured by locusts
The Jordan River would dry up
The sun would be darkened
explanation: 1 Kings 17:1 records Elijah saying: 'There shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.' (wrong_detail) Crops being devoured by locusts is a different plague, not part of Elijah's declaration here. (wrong_scope) The Jordan drying up is associated with a miracle in Elisha's ministry, not this drought proclamation. (common_misconception) The sun being darkened is imagery from a different type of calamity, not what Elijah announced.

content: After the brook Cherith dried up, to which city did God command Elijah to go so that a widow there would provide for him?
options: Zarephath
Samaria
Bethel
Jericho
explanation: 1 Kings 17:9 records the LORD saying: 'Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you.' (wrong_detail) Samaria was Ahab's capital, a place Elijah was avoiding rather than going to stay. (wrong_scope) Bethel was the northern center of golden-calf worship and has no connection to this passage. (near_passage) Jericho is associated with Elijah and Elisha's later activities, not the place where the widow provided for him.

content: During Queen Jezebel's persecution, what did Ahab's palace manager do to save the LORD's prophets?
options: He hid a hundred prophets in caves and supplied them with bread and water
He smuggled the prophets away to the land of Sidon
He disguised the prophets as the king's soldiers
He released the prophets into the wilderness
explanation: 1 Kings 18:4 records that Obadiah 'took a hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water.' (wrong_scope) Sidon was Jezebel's own homeland, so sending prophets there would have been senseless. (wrong_detail) The text says nothing about disguising them as soldiers; it says only that he hid them in caves. (common_misconception) Releasing them into the wilderness would have led to their deaths, the very opposite of Obadiah's protective intent.

content: Where did Elijah tell Ahab to assemble all Israel and the prophets of Baal for the contest?
options: Mount Carmel
Mount Horeb
Mount Sinai
Mount Zion
explanation: 1 Kings 18:19 records Elijah saying: 'Now therefore send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel.' (near_passage) Mount Horeb is where Elijah met God after this event (chapter 19), not the site of the contest. (wrong_scope) Mount Sinai is associated with Moses and the giving of the law, placing it outside the scope of this passage. (common_misconception) Mount Zion is in Jerusalem in the southern kingdom of Judah and was not the location of the challenge against Baal.

content: On Mount Carmel, what was Elijah's purpose in emphasizing the numerical contrast between himself and the prophets of Baal?
options: To show he stood alone against four hundred and fifty, so that any miracle would clearly display God's power
To suggest the people should fairly choose the larger side between the two groups
To persuade King Ahab to quickly recruit more prophets for the LORD's side
To ask the people for sympathy because he felt hopelessly outnumbered by the other prophets
explanation: 1 Kings 18:22 records Elijah saying: 'I, even I only, am left a prophet of the LORD, but Baal's prophets are 450 men.' His point was that when fire fell, it would unmistakably be God's power at work and not the result of superior numbers (wrong_detail). (common_misconception) He was not calling the people to follow the majority; on the contrary, the majority were on Baal's side. (wrong_scope) The text contains no request for Ahab to recruit additional prophets. (true_but_off) While he was indeed vastly outnumbered, his purpose was not to seek pity but to bring glory to God.

content: When the prophets of Baal cried out all day without any answer, what did Elijah mock them by suggesting about their god?
options: Perhaps their god was meditating, away on a journey, or asleep and needed to be called louder
Perhaps their god had already died, so it would be better for them to stop calling out
Perhaps their god was angry with them because the offering they had presented was not yet large enough
Perhaps their god was busy helping another nation and therefore could not hear them
explanation: 1 Kings 18:27 records Elijah mocking them: 'Cry aloud, for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened.' (wrong_detail) Elijah told them to cry louder — he did not tell them to stop calling because their god had died. (common_misconception) He never said the god was angry because the offering was too small; his mockery was aimed at the god's powerlessness. (wrong_scope) The idea of helping another nation does not appear in the text — it is a reading beyond what the verse actually says.

content: Before praying for fire to fall, why did Elijah command that water be poured over the sacrifice and the wood three times?
options: To eliminate any suspicion of hidden fire, so that the miracle would be undeniable
To make the wood on the altar burn more slowly and longer when the fire fell
To cleanse the sacrifice in accordance with the ritual requirements of the law before presenting it
To fill the trench around the altar completely so that the people could drink the water
explanation: 1 Kings 18:33-35 records that Elijah had water poured three times until the water ran around the altar and filled the trench also. The purpose was to make the fire consuming even the water an undeniable miracle (wrong_detail). (common_misconception) Water makes burning more difficult — it does not cause the wood to burn longer. (true_but_off) Although cleansing the sacrifice was a genuine ritual practice in the law, that is not the reason here; this was a demonstration of the true God in contrast to Baal. (wrong_scope) The trench held water to prove the miracle, not to provide drinking water for the people.

content: When the son of the widow of Zarephath died, what did her cry of distress reveal she had misunderstood about Elijah's presence?
options: She believed the man of God had come to expose her sin, bringing about her son's death
She believed Elijah had stolen her son to offer him as a sacrifice
She believed Elijah was powerless and that Baal had acted instead
She believed her son died because she had shared bread with Elijah and exhausted her food supply
explanation: 1 Kings 17:18 records her saying: 'What have you against me, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!' (wrong_scope) Nothing in the text suggests she thought Elijah had stolen her son to offer as a sacrifice. (common_misconception) She did not blame Baal; she acknowledged Elijah as a man of God. (wrong_detail) The flour and oil had not run out because of the earlier miracle, so running out of food was not part of her complaint.

content: Compared to the episode of fire falling from heaven, what difference in Elijah's manner of action does the return of rain after the drought reveal?
options: The fire came instantly after a single prayer, while the rain came after Elijah bowed himself down to pray and sent his servant to look toward the sea seven times
Both miracles came instantly right after Elijah's first prayer
The fire came after seven prayers, while the rain came immediately when he looked up
The rain came because Elijah poured water on the altar, while the fire came because he sent his servant to look at the sky
explanation: 1 Kings 18:36-38 shows the fire fell immediately after Elijah's prayer, while 18:42-44 records him bowing with his face between his knees and sending his servant to look seven times until a small cloud appeared. (wrong_detail) It is not the case that both came instantly; the rain required persistent prayer. (wrong_detail) This reverses the order — it was the rain that came after seven lookings, not the fire. (common_misconception) The details are confused: pouring water belongs to the fire episode, while looking seven times belongs to the rain episode — they cannot be swapped as this option suggests.

content: Considering the two phases of God's provision for Elijah during the drought, in what main way does the miracle of sustenance at Zarephath differ from the miracle at the Cherith Brook?
options: At Cherith, God provided through ravens, while at Zarephath He provided through a widow with flour and oil that never ran out
At both places, God used ravens to bring bread and meat to sustain Elijah regularly every day
At Cherith, God used a widow to feed him, while at Zarephath God used ravens to supply him daily
At Zarephath the brook never ran dry, while at Cherith the flour and oil never ran out
explanation: 1 Kings 17:4-6 records that at Cherith the ravens brought bread and meat while Elijah drank from the brook; 17:14-16 records that at Zarephath a widow cared for him and 'the jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty.' The difference is provision directly through nature versus through a human being together with the miracle of flour and oil (wrong_detail). (wrong_detail) It is not true that both places involved ravens; at Zarephath the provision was through a widow. (wrong_detail) This option reverses the two locations — the widow was at Zarephath and the ravens were at Cherith. (common_misconception) The miracles are confused: the brook running dry was at Cherith, while the flour and oil not running out was at Zarephath — assigning them in reverse is incorrect.

content: When fleeing into the wilderness, Elijah sat down to rest under what kind of tree and prayed that he might die?
options: A juniper (broom tree)
A fig tree by the roadside
A fruit-bearing olive tree
A shady oak tree
explanation: According to 1 Kings 19:4, Elijah went a day's journey into the wilderness, sat down under a broom tree (juniper), and asked that he might die. The fig tree is a wrong textual detail, associated with other images in Scripture (wrong_detail). The olive tree does not appear in this scene (wrong_detail). The oak tree is typically associated with other scenes such as those involving Abraham, not this one (wrong_scope).

content: Who woke Elijah while he was sleeping and brought him food and water so he would have enough strength for the journey?
options: An angel
The prophet Elisha
The widow of Zarephath
Elijah's servant
explanation: According to 1 Kings 19:5-7, an angel touched Elijah, told him to arise and eat, and had set out a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water; with the strength from that food he traveled forty days to Mount Horeb. Elisha had not yet been called at this point, so he could not be this person (wrong_scope). The widow of Zarephath belongs to the earlier story in chapter 17 (wrong_scope). Elijah's servant had been left behind at Beersheba before Elijah went into the wilderness (wrong_detail).

content: How many days and nights did Elijah travel to reach the mountain of God?
options: Forty days and forty nights
Three days and three nights
Seven days and seven nights
Twenty days and twenty nights
explanation: According to 1 Kings 19:8, strengthened by that food, Elijah traveled forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. Three days and three nights is a number associated with other scenes in Scripture and does not apply here (wrong_detail). Seven days and seven nights is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). Twenty days is a completely incorrect number (wrong_detail).

content: At Horeb, the LORD told Elijah to anoint whom as king over Syria (Aram)?
options: Hazael
Jehu
Ben-Hadad
Naaman
explanation: According to 1 Kings 19:15, the LORD told Elijah to anoint Hazael as king over Syria. Jehu is mentioned in the very next verse but as king over Israel, not Syria (near_passage). Ben-Hadad was the reigning king of Syria and was not the one anointed to replace him (wrong_detail). Naaman was a commander of the Syrian army in a later story involving Elisha and is unrelated here (wrong_scope).

content: According to the LORD's word to Elijah, why were the anointings of Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha a linked trio?
options: The three would successively execute judgment: whoever escaped the sword of one would be killed by the next
The three would jointly rule all of Israel, forming a three-king alliance
The three would all become prophets to succeed Elijah at the school of the prophets after his death
The three would together go and destroy all the remaining prophets of Baal still in the land
explanation: According to 1 Kings 19:17, the LORD declared that whoever escaped the sword of Hazael would be killed by Jehu, and whoever escaped the sword of Jehu would be killed by Elisha; the three form a successive chain of judgment. The option 'jointly rule as a three-king alliance' is wrong because Elisha was a prophet, not a king (wrong_detail). The option 'all become prophets to succeed Elijah' applies only to Elisha; it is wrong for the other two, who were kings (wrong_detail). The option 'together go and destroy the prophets of Baal' conflates this commission with the victory at Carmel in the previous chapter, which was not the purpose of this trio (near_passage).

content: After being called by Elijah, what did Elisha do with the pair of oxen he was plowing with to demonstrate his decisive commitment to following the LORD?
options: Slaughtered the oxen, used the yoke as firewood to cook the meat, and fed the people
Sold the oxen and gave the money to the temple, then set out on his way
Left the oxen with his parents and quietly followed Elijah
Brought the oxen along to offer as a sacrifice at Horeb
explanation: According to 1 Kings 19:21, Elisha took the pair of oxen and slaughtered them, used the plowing equipment as firewood to cook the meat, and gave it to the people to eat before he arose and followed Elijah, serving him — showing that he severed ties with his former livelihood. 'Selling the oxen and giving the money to the temple' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Leaving the oxen with his parents and quietly leaving' is incorrect because while he did ask to take leave of his parents, he slaughtered the oxen rather than leaving them behind (near_passage). 'Bringing the oxen to offer as a sacrifice at Horeb' confuses the location with Horeb from the preceding passage and misrepresents the action (wrong_scope).

content: Which king allied with thirty-two other kings to march up and besiege Samaria?
options: Ben-Hadad king of Syria
Hazael king of Syria
Pharaoh king of Egypt
Sennacherib king of Assyria
explanation: According to 1 Kings 20:1, Ben-Hadad king of Syria mustered all his army, with thirty-two kings supporting him, and marched up to besiege Samaria against Ahab. Hazael was also king of Syria but only came to the throne later and is not the figure in this event (wrong_detail). Pharaoh of Egypt had no part in this siege (wrong_scope). Sennacherib of Assyria belongs to a much later period and is unrelated to this chapter (wrong_scope).

content: In the first battle against the Syrians, which of Ahab's forces was directed by the prophet's word to strike first?
options: The young men (servants) of the district governors
Ahab's entire cavalry and chariot force
The priests blowing trumpets as they marched around the city
Philistine mercenaries hired for the campaign
explanation: According to 1 Kings 20:14-15, the prophet told Ahab that the young men of the district governors would begin the battle; Ahab mustered them and counted two hundred and thirty-two men, and they went out first. 'Ahab's entire cavalry and chariot force' is incorrect because it was the Syrians who possessed the great chariot strength; Ahab led the attack with this small company of young men (wrong_detail). 'Priests blowing trumpets marching around the city' confuses this with the battle of Jericho under Joshua (wrong_scope). 'Philistine mercenaries' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: After their first defeat, Syria's advisors argued that Ahab should be fought on the plains; why then did the LORD determine to give Israel a second victory on those very plains?
options: To prove that He is LORD of both hills and valleys, refuting the notion that He is only a god of the hills
To reward King Ahab because he had genuinely repented and returned to worship the LORD wholeheartedly
Because on the plains Israel's chariots were stronger, making victory easier than in the highlands
Because Ben-Hadad had broken his promise and refused to return the cities he had pledged to give back to Ahab
explanation: According to 1 Kings 20:23, the servants of Syria said that Israel's God is a god of the hills, which is why they lost, and that fighting on the plains would bring victory; but in 20:28 the man of God announced that the LORD would deliver that great army into Ahab's hand 'that you may know that I am the LORD,' thereby refuting the notion that He rules only the hills. 'Rewarding Ahab for wholehearted repentance' is wrong because Ahab remained an evil king; the stated purpose is explicitly to reveal who the LORD is (common_misconception). 'Israel's chariots being stronger on the plains' reverses the text: it was the Syrians who trusted in their chariot force on flat terrain (wrong_detail). 'Because Ben-Hadad broke his promise to restore the cities' belongs to the later negotiation episode and is not the reason given for the second victory (near_passage).

content: What method did the prophet use to cause Ahab to pronounce judgment on himself for having spared Ben-Hadad's life?
options: Disguised himself as a wounded soldier, told a story about letting a prisoner escape, and let Ahab pronounce the penalty himself
Confronted Ahab directly in the royal court and declared the LORD's judgment against him
Wrote a warning on the wall of the palace for Ahab to read and come to his senses
Sent a child to read the LORD's rebuke before the king and his officials
explanation: According to 1 Kings 20:38-42, the prophet disguised himself with a bandage over his eyes, stood by the road waiting for the king, and told a story about being entrusted with a prisoner who escaped, making him liable to pay with his life; Ahab pronounced that very verdict, and the prophet then revealed himself and applied that judgment to the king for having released Ben-Hadad. 'Confronting him directly in the royal court' is wrong because the key element was the covert entrapment through a disguised parable (wrong_detail). 'Writing words on the palace wall' confuses this with the vision of the hand writing on the wall in the book of Daniel (wrong_scope). 'Sending a child to read God's rebuke' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: Which piece of land near the palace in Jezreel did King Ahab covet so much that he became sullen and refused to eat?
options: A vineyard
A grain field
An olive grove
A well
explanation: According to 1 Kings 21:1-2, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard next to Ahab's palace, and the king wanted to take it for a vegetable garden. 'A grain field' is wrong about the type of land (wrong_detail). 'An olive grove' is a different kind of planting not mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). 'A well' was not the object of the dispute (wrong_detail).

content: When Naboth refused to give up his land, how did King Ahab react when he returned home?
options: He was sullen, lay down on his bed with his face turned to the wall, and refused to eat
He immediately ordered Naboth to be executed on the spot
He prayed to God to judge and decide the matter
He summoned soldiers to surround Naboth's house
explanation: According to 1 Kings 21:4, Ahab went home resentful and sullen, lay on his bed with his face to the wall, and refused to eat. 'Executing Naboth' was a later act carried out through Jezebel's scheme, not Ahab's immediate response (wrong_scope). 'Praying to God' contradicts Ahab's character as portrayed in the text (common_misconception). 'Summoning soldiers' did not occur (wrong_detail).

content: In her plot against Naboth, what legal scheme did Jezebel arrange to create grounds for having him killed?
options: She hired two scoundrels to give false testimony that Naboth had cursed God and the king
She charged Naboth with a large tax debt and used it as grounds to seize his land
She accused Naboth of secretly and unlawfully worshiping Baal in the land
She alleged that Naboth had secretly conspired with the king of Syria in an act of treason
explanation: According to 1 Kings 21:8-10, Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name instructing the elders to seat two worthless men opposite Naboth to charge that he had cursed God and the king, so that he could be stoned to death. 'Charging a tax debt' is an economic accusation not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Secretly worshiping Baal unlawfully' reverses reality, since it was Ahab's own house that worshiped Baal (common_misconception). 'Conspiring with the king of Syria' is a charge of treason applied to the wrong context (wrong_detail).

content: What punishment did the prophet Elijah declare upon Ahab himself at the very place where dogs had licked Naboth's blood?
options: Dogs would also lick Ahab's blood in that same place
Lightning would strike and burn down the king's palace
The king would be exiled to Babylon
The king would be struck blind until the day of his death
explanation: According to 1 Kings 21:19, Elijah declared that in the place where dogs licked Naboth's blood, dogs would also lick Ahab's blood. 'Lightning burning the palace' is the wrong kind of punishment and is absent from the proclamation (wrong_detail). 'Exile to Babylon' confuses this with Judah's later fate and is wrong in scope (wrong_scope). 'Being struck blind' is a punishment wrongly attributed here (wrong_detail).

content: After Elijah's warning, Ahab tore his clothes and put on sackcloth; how did God adjust the announced judgment in response to his humbling himself?
options: He deferred the disaster upon Ahab's house to the days of Ahab's son
He completely canceled all the punishments that had been declared
He postponed the punishment until Jezebel died
He transferred the punishment to the elders of Jezreel
explanation: According to 1 Kings 21:27-29, because Ahab humbled himself, God declared He would not bring the disaster during Ahab's lifetime but in his son's days. 'Completely canceling' is wrong because the judgment was deferred, not annulled — this is the critical distinction (common_misconception). 'Postponing until Jezebel died' assigns the wrong time marker; the text specifies his son's days (wrong_detail). 'Transferring to the elders' invents a different recipient of punishment — plausible since they were complicit, but not what God declared (true_but_off).

content: Which city, then in the hand of the king of Syria, did Ahab invite King Jehoshaphat of Judah to help him recapture?
options: Ramoth-gilead
Damascus of Syria
Samaria in the north
Jericho near the Jordan River
explanation: According to 1 Kings 22:3–4, Ahab said that Ramoth-gilead belonged to them and invited Jehoshaphat to go with him to take it back from the king of Syria. 'Damascus' was the capital of Syria, not the military objective (wrong_detail). 'Samaria' was Ahab's own capital (wrong_detail). 'Jericho' belonged to a different territory and had no connection to this battle (wrong_scope).

content: Why did King Ahab express hatred toward the prophet Micaiah son of Imlah when Jehoshaphat asked to inquire of another prophet of the LORD?
options: Because Micaiah never prophesied good concerning Ahab, but always evil
Because Micaiah had previously and flatly refused to anoint Ahab as king
Because Micaiah was a Syrian who belonged to the side of the king's enemies
Because Micaiah had publicly bowed down and worshiped Baal before all the people
explanation: According to 1 Kings 22:8, Ahab said he hated Micaiah because the prophet never prophesied good concerning him, but always evil. 'Refusing to anoint him' invents an event not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'A Syrian belonging to the enemy's side' misidentifies his origin, since Micaiah was a prophet of the LORD (wrong_detail). 'Worshiping Baal' reverses roles — that was what Ahab did, not Micaiah (common_misconception).

content: What symbolic object did the prophet Zedekiah son of Chenaanah use to encourage Ahab that he would defeat the Syrians?
options: A pair of iron horns he had made himself
A gold-plated sword
A bow broken in two
A bundle of arrows set ablaze
explanation: According to 1 Kings 22:11, Zedekiah made himself horns of iron and declared that with them the king would gore the Syrians until they were destroyed. 'A gold-plated sword' is a fabricated prop not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'A bow broken in two' suggests defeat, which directly contradicts his message of victory (wrong_detail). 'A bundle of burning arrows' confuses this with the symbolic act of another prophet and falls outside this passage (wrong_scope).

content: Ahab disguised himself before going into battle in an attempt to escape his appointed fate — what event showed that this plan failed?
options: A man drew his bow at random and struck the king between the joints of his armor
The Syrian troops recognized the king by his crown and surrounded him
Jehoshaphat was wearing his royal robes and was killed in Ahab's place
Zedekiah betrayed Ahab and revealed the king's hiding place to the enemy
explanation: According to 1 Kings 22:30–34, even though Ahab disguised himself, a man drew his bow at random and struck the king at the joint of his armor, showing that no disguise could escape the judgment the LORD had decreed. 'Recognized by his crown' contradicts the fact that he had disguised himself to conceal his identity (wrong_detail). 'Jehoshaphat killed in his place' is incorrect — Jehoshaphat cried out and was spared, surviving the battle (wrong_detail). 'Zedekiah betraying and pointing out his hiding place' invents an action not in the text, and Zedekiah was among those urging the king to go to war (wrong_scope).

content: When Ahab's chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria, what happened in fulfillment of the word of the LORD?
options: Dogs licked up the king's blood
The water of the pool turned to blood
Ravens carried away the king's body
Fire from heaven consumed the chariot
explanation: According to 1 Kings 22:38, when the chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria, dogs licked up Ahab's blood, fulfilling the word the LORD had spoken. 'The pool turning to blood' confuses this with the plague in Egypt and falls outside this context (wrong_scope). 'Ravens carrying away his body' is a fabricated detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Fire from heaven consuming the chariot' confuses this with a different miracle of Elijah and is the wrong context (wrong_scope).
